title: Ten sayings (Avot 5:1)
hookLine: the world was made with ten sayings, so that each life counts
tomorrow: what did God make at sunset, right before the first Shabbat?

lines: AND GOD SAID, AND GOD SAID.
cards: Some things could be done in one step and aren't. A letter written by hand instead of a text. A cake from scratch instead of a box.

Avot notices that about the world itself. Genesis tells creation as a string of sayings: and God said, and God said. Chapter five opens by counting ten of them, then asks the question a kid would ask.
Couldn't it have been made with one?

teach.h: TEN, SO THE WORLD WEIGHS MORE.
teach.b: The mishnah answers itself. Ten, so the world would weigh more: so the wicked, who destroy a world made with ten sayings, pay for it, and the righteous, who sustain a world made with ten sayings, get good reward.
Something to tell a friend tonight: count the and God saids in Genesis one and you get nine. The Talmud noticed, and says in the beginning is a saying too.
Now the two readings, because people lean two ways on one sentence.
One side hears a warning. The world was made with care, step by step, so breaking any part of it is serious; carelessness costs more than it looks. The other side hears an invitation.
If the world took ten sayings, then holding up even a small piece of it, a meal, a kept promise, a kind word, carries that weight too. The mishnah puts both in one breath and doesn't choose.
Another mishnah, in Sanhedrin, makes it personal.
One person was created alone, it says, to teach that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever sustains one life, as if they sustained a whole world.
And one more reason: so no one could say to another, my ancestor is greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same one.

how: Pirkei Avot is read on summer Shabbat afternoons, a chapter a week; chapter five's numbered sayings, of tens, sevens and fours, are often studied in pairs, with partners arguing over each reading.

o: ten rules for speaking with kindness
the words God spoke to make the world
the Ten Commandments given at Sinai

games.q: chapter five, the first saying — tap the pairs.
p: destroy a world made with care
sustain a world made with care

s: the ten sayings of Avot 5:1 are the Ten Commandments
these are the sayings of creation: and God said, in Genesis.
the same mishnah asks whether the world could have been made with one saying
it asks, and answers: ten, so that what we do to the world weighs more.
in Genesis 1, 'and God said' appears ten times
the Talmud counts nine, and calls 'in the beginning' a saying too.

games.q: your study partner says Avot 5:1 is a warning: don't wreck what was made with care. she asks you to argue the other side as well as you can. what do you say?
o: it's an invitation too: holding up any small piece of the world carries the weight of ten sayings.
there is no other side; the mishnah only talks about what happens to the wicked.
the other side is that the number ten is symbolic, so the saying has no real point.
games.why: the mishnah names both: those who destroy and those who sustain a world made with ten sayings. the best case for the other side is already in the sentence.

practice: Say one good sentence out loud, about someone in your life, plainly, the way you'd say it to their face. Then another, about someone else.
Keep going for as long as the sit holds, up to ten, each one a small saying that holds a piece of the world up.
